title: THE MOMENT YOU THINK YOU’RE BETTER THAN EVERYONE ELSE, YOU MAY BE FARTHER FROM JESUS THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: THE MOMENT YOU THINK YOU’RE BETTER THAN EVERYONE ELSE, YOU MAY BE FARTHER FROM JESUS THAN YOU THINK
The frightening story Jesus told about a religious man who looked righteous, prayed correctly, lived morally—and still walked away unjustified.
There is a kind of sin that rarely feels like sin.
It does not stumble into church smelling like alcohol.
It does not arrive with scandal written across its face.
It knows the songs.
It carries a Bible.
It can quote Scripture.
It may serve, give, fast, pray, preach, correct theology, defend Christian morality, and warn everybody else about compromise.
And that is exactly why it can be so dangerous.
Because some sins make you ashamed enough to run toward Jesus.
This one can make you feel righteous enough to believe you no longer desperately need Him.
Read that again.

There may come a moment in your Christian life when you look at somebody else's marriage, addiction, failure, clothing, parenting, theology, finances, past, church attendance, political opinions, sexual sin, temper, weakness, or reputation—and something almost invisible happens inside you.
You do not necessarily say anything.
You just think...
“At least I’m not like them.”
And somewhere in that sentence, a throne is being built.
Jesus once told a story about two men who walked into the same place to pray.
One looked respectable.
The other carried a reputation people despised.
One could present an impressive spiritual résumé.
The other could barely present himself.
And Jesus deliberately made the ending uncomfortable.
Luke tells us that Jesus spoke the parable specifically to people who “trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (Luke 18:9).
That description matters.
Their problem was not merely confidence.
Their confidence had found the wrong foundation.
They trusted in themselves.
Then self-righteousness produced its predictable offspring:
contempt.
Jesus continues:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18:10).
To modern ears, “Pharisee” can immediately sound like “villain.”
That can cause us to miss the shock.
The Pharisee was the visibly religious man.
The tax collector belonged to a profession widely despised in Jewish society under Roman rule and associated with exploitation and collaboration.
If you had been standing nearby judging the two men by reputation alone, you might have expected the Pharisee to be the spiritual success story.
Then he began praying.
In the Greek text of Luke 18:11 we encounter these devastating words:
“ὁ θεὸς, εὐχαριστῶ σοι ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ ὥσπερ οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων...”
“God, I thank You that I am not like the rest of mankind...”
At first, it almost sounds like gratitude.
“God, I thank You...”
But listen to what his gratitude becomes.
A comparison.
He begins talking to God while measuring himself against people.
He mentions extortioners, unjust people, adulterers.
Then his eyes land on the man standing nearby.
“...or even like this tax collector.”
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because you do not have to say those exact words to pray the Pharisee’s prayer.
“Thank God my children didn't turn out like theirs.”
“Thank God I understand Scripture better than those people.”
“Thank God I would never fall into that sin.”
“Thank God I’m not one of those lukewarm Christians.”
“Thank God my church actually teaches truth.”
“Thank God I’m not like him.”
“Thank God I’m not like her.”
And perhaps the most dangerous version:
“Thank God I’m not like that Pharisee.”
There it is.
Pride is so deceptive that we can become proud of recognizing pride in somebody else.
The Pharisee continues by listing his spiritual achievements.
He fasts.
He tithes.
Those actions themselves were not the problem.
Fasting can honor God.
Giving can honor God.
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
Jesus was not condemning faithfulness.
He was exposing what happens when obedience stops producing gratitude and starts producing superiority.
There is an enormous difference between saying:
“Jesus has been merciful to me.”
and quietly believing:
“Jesus must be impressed with me.”
Then Jesus moves our attention toward the other man.
The tax collector stands at a distance.
He will not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beats his breast.
And his prayer is painfully short.
Luke 18:13 records:
“ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.”
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
No résumé.
No comparison.
No excuses.
No explanation of childhood trauma.
No list of people worse than him.
No bargaining.
No attempt to impress heaven.
Just a sinner who finally understands that his greatest hope is not that somebody else is worse.
His hope is mercy.
And this is where Jesus overturns the room.
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other...” (Luke 18:14).
The scandalous man goes home justified.
The respectable man does not.
Why?
Not because sin suddenly became irrelevant.
Not because repentance does not matter.
Not because righteousness does not matter.
The tax collector understood something the Pharisee had forgotten:
You cannot rescue yourself.
The Gospel does not begin with how much better you are becoming than everybody else.
It begins with how desperately you need a Savior.
That is why Christianity leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
Paul asks one of the most pride-destroying questions in the New Testament:
“τί δὲ ἔχεις ὃ οὐκ ἔλαβες;”
“What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).
Think about that.
Your breath?
Received.
Your intelligence?
Received.
Your opportunities?
Received.
Your ability to read Scripture?
Received.
The people who discipled you?
Grace.
The conviction that brought you to repentance?
Grace.
The strength that helped you resist temptation yesterday?
Grace.
The forgiveness covering sins you would be horrified to see projected publicly?
Grace.
The cross?
Grace.
The empty tomb?
Grace.
The promise of eternal life?
Grace upon grace.
So what exactly are we boasting about?
The Gospel does not tell you that you are superior.
It tells you that you were helpless enough to need the blood of the Son of God.
That should destroy both despair and arrogance at the same time.
You cannot say, “I am too filthy for Jesus,” because His grace is greater than your sin.
But you also cannot stand at Calvary and say, “I am better than those people,” because the cross announces that you needed saving too.
At the foot of the cross, nobody has an impressive résumé.
We arrive as sinners.
We survive by mercy.
We stand by grace.
This is why Paul writes in Romans 12:3 not to think of ourselves “more highly” than we ought to think.
And Philippians 2:3 presses even deeper:
“μηδὲν κατὰ ἐριθείαν μηδὲ κατὰ κενοδοξίαν...”
“Do nothing from selfish ambition or empty conceit...”
The Greek word κενοδοξία carries the idea of empty or vain glory.
Empty glory.
That is such an accurate picture of pride.
We spend years constructing trophies heaven never asked us to win.
Better Christian.
Better parent.
Better theologian.
Better church member.
Better husband.
Better wife.
Better preacher.
Better denomination.
Better testimony.
Better morality.
Better understanding.
Better than them.
Then Jesus walks into our carefully constructed ranking system and asks a question that makes every trophy suddenly feel hollow:
Who gave you what you have?
That does not mean Christians should pretend truth and error are identical.
They are not.
Jesus confronted sin.
The apostles confronted false teaching.
Scripture commands discernment.
Biblical humility is not moral confusion.
You can call sin what God calls sin without treating the sinner as though you never needed mercy yourself.
You can defend truth without worshiping your own correctness.
You can confront someone without enjoying their humiliation.
You can disagree without despising.
You can pursue holiness without turning holiness into a ladder from which you look down on everyone underneath you.
And perhaps this is where it hurts.
Sometimes we do not actually want restoration for the person who fell.
We want confirmation that we were better than them all along.
Someone's marriage collapses, and secretly we feel validated.
A pastor falls publicly, and somewhere beneath our righteous anger is a whisper:
“I knew something was wrong with him.”
Someone who criticized us fails, and their pain almost tastes like vindication.
A struggling believer confesses the same sin again, and compassion slowly becomes irritation.
We forget how patient Jesus has been with us.
We remember people's worst chapters while asking God to remember ours no more.
We demand justice for their sins and mercy for our own.
That is not the heart of Christ.
Imagine if Jesus treated you according to the standard you sometimes use on everyone else.
Imagine if every secret thought were exposed.
Every jealous impulse.
Every lustful glance.
Every dishonest motive.
Every prayer performed for appearances.
Every moment you wanted recognition.
Every private bitterness.
Every act of obedience secretly hoping somebody would notice.
Every time you judged another person's visible battle while protecting your invisible one.
Would you still feel superior?
This is why grace is so offensive to human pride.
Grace means the person you judged can be forgiven.
Grace means the addict can become your brother.
The prostitute can become your sister.
The prisoner can become a preacher.
The prodigal can come home.
The religious hypocrite can repent.
The person whose life became a public scandal can kneel before Jesus and rise covered by a righteousness they could never manufacture.
And so can you.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people proving themselves worthy.
Not bad people learning to behave impressively.
Sinners reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
Christ forgives.
Christ transforms.
And because salvation is rooted in Him, there is no room left for boasting as though we accomplished our own resurrection.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest scandal is the pride you have hidden beneath religious respectability.
Jesus is still calling you away from self-righteousness and toward grace.
Repentance does not mean pretending sin is small.
Repentance means finally agreeing with God about it and turning toward the One who can forgive and transform you.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it only needs to be honest.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
That prayer is not weakness.
It is the collapse of an illusion.
You were never saved because you were better.
You were saved because Jesus is merciful.
And when you truly understand that, something changes in the way you see people.
The broken person stops being merely disgusting and becomes someone who needs the Savior you needed.
The struggling Christian stops being merely frustrating and becomes someone who needs the patience Christ repeatedly gives you.
The unbeliever stops being your enemy to defeat and becomes a soul for whom Christ calls His people to bear witness.
The fallen believer becomes someone who may need correction, repentance, accountability—and restoration.
And you?
You stop needing everybody beneath you in order to feel secure.
Your identity is no longer built on being better than them.
It is built on belonging to Him.
That is freedom.
Who have I been looking down on?
Do not answer for your spouse.
Do not answer for your pastor.
Do not answer for the person whose hypocrisy irritates you.
Answer for yourself.
Whose name came into your mind?
That person may be exactly where Jesus wants to expose something in your heart.
Not so He can destroy you.
So He can free you.
You can simply write, “Jesus, humble me.”
If you have been fighting pride and you are tired of measuring your life against everyone else's, comment, “Grace, not pride.”
If you need prayer because your heart has grown hard toward somebody, comment, “pray for me.”

And if Christ has already rescued you from a season when you thought you were beyond restoration, tell somebody what His grace did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed before giving up.
Not because you need another saved post buried in a folder, but because pride has a remarkable ability to return after conviction fades.
Come back when you are tempted to believe somebody else's failure makes you righteous.
But if Gospel Warrior is genuinely helping you follow Christ, supporting and sharing this work can be one practical way to help these messages reach people who may never walk through a church door.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
a tax collector who desperately needs mercy...
a wounded Christian who thinks the church has no place left for them...
or a sinner who has never understood that Jesus receives people who come to Him empty-handed.
And before you judge which one of them needs this most...
remember the story.
Two men entered the temple.
One carried an impressive record.
One carried nothing but repentance.
Only one went home justified.
The most dangerous distance from Jesus may not begin when you realize how sinful you are.
It may begin when you become convinced that everybody else's sin has made you righteous.
So come down from the pedestal.
There is room at the foot of the cross.
There always was.
Because when everything we used to prove that we were better finally falls from our hands, we discover something infinitely better waiting there:
Jesus.
Mercy for the guilty.
Grace for the proud.
Forgiveness for the repentant.
A new heart for the surrendered.
And a completely rewritten ending for anyone who comes to Christ.
Never forget this:
The moment you stop needing grace because you think you are better than everyone else may be the very moment you need grace to open your eyes again.
